nameStory: This grass gets its unusual name from the warty, bumpy texture of its seeds and flowering parts that you can actually feel when you run your fingers over them. The word "panic" comes from the Latin "panicum," referring to a type of millet - many grasses in this family were once called panic grasses because of their loose, branching flower clusters.
description: Warty panic grass is a native perennial grass that forms small tufts or clumps, typically growing 1-3 feet tall. It has narrow, flat leaves and produces loose, open clusters of tiny flowers on delicate branching stems. The plant gets its distinctive name from the noticeably bumpy, warty texture of its seeds and flower parts. This is one of our less common native grasses, making it an exciting find for grass enthusiasts.

idTips.label: Seeds/Flowers
idTips.description: The seeds and tiny flower parts have a distinctly warty, bumpy texture that you can feel when you gently roll them between your fingers - this is the plant's signature feature

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small, neat tufts or clumps 1-3 feet tall rather than spreading into large patches like many other grasses

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, flat leaves that are typically 2-6 inches long with a smooth texture and parallel veins like most grasses

idTips.label: Flower Clusters
idTips.description: Produces loose, open, branching clusters of tiny flowers on delicate stems that sway gently in the breeze

habitat: Look for warty panic grass in dry, sandy soils and open woodlands, particularly in areas with some disturbance or edge habitat. It often grows along woodland borders, in clearings, or on sandy slopes where other vegetation is sparse. This grass prefers well-drained soils and can tolerate drought conditions once established.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge and leaves begin growing. The plant forms its characteristic small clumps as it comes out of winter dormancy.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs from mid to late summer, when the distinctive warty seed heads develop and become most noticeable for identification.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and the warty texture becomes most pronounced. Leaves may begin to turn golden or brown as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back to brown, dried stems and leaves. The plant survives as underground roots and crowns, ready to regrow in spring.

funFact: This grass is so uncommon that it's been documented only 10 times in all of New England, making every sighting a genuine botanical treasure - you're more likely to spot a rare bird than this elusive grass!
confusionNotes: With only 10 recorded observations in New England, this grass is rarely confused with anything simply because so few people encounter it. When found, the warty seed texture is usually distinctive enough to separate it from other small panic grasses.
contextualKnowledge: The genus Kellochloa was recently separated from the larger Panicum genus based on genetic studies, so you might find this species listed as Panicum verrucosum in older field guides or botanical references.
compareHints: Since warty panic grass is the only Kellochloa species in our region, compare it to other small panic grasses by focusing on the distinctive warty seed texture - most similar grasses have smooth seeds. The tufted growth habit also helps distinguish it from spreading panic grass species that form larger colonies.
